title: You would think wisdom would be enough.
paragraphs:
You would think wisdom would be enough.
That once a man has seen clearly—really seen—he would never go back.
But that’s not what happened.
And if you’re honest… it’s not what’s happening to you either.
Because there are things you already know are wrong—and you still do them.
You’ve felt the conviction before.
You’ve heard the truth.
You’ve even agreed with it.
And yet… you went back.
Solomon understood that tension better than anyone.
This was not a foolish man. This was the man God Himself gave wisdom to beyond measure. Scripture says no one like him had ever lived before in wisdom, and none would come after. Kings traveled across nations just to hear him speak. He wrote proverbs that still cut to the heart today.
He knew truth.
He could discern right from wrong with precision.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
He didn’t follow it.
The moment that exposes everything is quiet—but devastating:
“For when Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and his heart was not fully true to the Lord his God…” (1 Kings 11:4)
Read that again.
Not “he didn’t know.”
Not “he was confused.”
Not “he lacked wisdom.”
His heart was not fully true.
That’s the fracture.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
You can know the right thing—and still choose the wrong one.
You can quote Scripture—and still disobey it.
You can give advice to others—and secretly ignore it in your own life.
God saw it.
You knew.
Solomon didn’t fall because he lacked understanding.
He fell because he stopped guarding his heart.
Somewhere along the way, knowledge became something he possessed—but not something that possessed him.
And that’s where the danger lives.
Because wisdom, when it doesn’t lead to obedience, becomes deception.
You start believing you’re spiritually safe… just because you understand spiritual things.
But Scripture doesn’t say, “Be hearers only.”
It says:
“Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.” (James 1:22)
Deceiving yourselves.
Not being deceived by others.
Self-deception.
That means you can sit in truth… and still be lost in it.
Solomon built temples, wrote Scripture, led a nation—and still let his heart drift into idolatry.
It didn’t happen overnight.
It was slow.
Compromise dressed as tolerance.
Disobedience disguised as complexity.
Attachment justified by emotion.
And eventually…
His heart belonged somewhere else.
This is where it gets uncomfortably close.
Because you’ve been telling yourself:
“I know better.”
But knowing better hasn’t stopped you.
You still entertain what God said to cut off.
You still justify what He already exposed.
You still delay obedience like it’s optional.
And every time you do…
Your heart moves.
Not loudly.
Not dramatically.
Quietly.
Until one day, like Solomon, you look back and realize—you’re not fully His anymore.
That’s the cost.
Not ignorance.
Drift.
There’s a reason Scripture warns:
“Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)
Solomon wrote that.
He knew it.
But he didn’t live it.
That’s the lesson.
And it should shake you.
Because if wisdom alone were enough, Solomon would have finished well.
But he didn’t.
And neither will you—if obedience is optional in your life.
This is where everything shifts.
Because the Gospel was never about knowing more.
It was about surrender.
Jesus didn’t die so you could become informed.
He died so you could be transformed.
“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?” (Luke 6:46)
That question doesn’t leave room to hide.
Because calling Him Lord means He has authority.
And authority demands response.
Not later.
Now.
The cross doesn’t just forgive your sin.
It confronts your rebellion.
It calls you out of partial devotion and into full surrender.
No divided heart.
No secret compromises.
No intellectual Christianity without real obedience.
Jesus didn’t carry the cross halfway.
And He’s not asking for half of you either.
So now you’re standing in that space again.
You know what God has been dealing with you about.
That thing you keep excusing.
That habit you keep returning to.
That compromise you keep minimizing.
This is the moment.
Not to learn more.
But to obey.
Because there are only two directions from here:
You either become someone who knows truth and follows it…
Or someone who knows truth and slowly walks away from it.
One leads to life.
The other looks wise—but ends in ruin.
Say it plainly.
Confess it.
Type it if you have to—“I knew, but I didn’t obey.”
Let it come into the light.
And if you’re ready to stop living in cycles of knowing without changing—there’s more waiting for you.
There’s deeper truth, sharper correction, and real discipleship inside the Gospel Warrior movement. Not surface-level content—but something that will press you, refine you, and anchor you in obedience.
Step into it here:

Because wisdom didn’t save Solomon.
But surrender still can save you.
